name: 6 - Solving Problems with the Public Transcript
content:
WEBVTT
 
 Aline Muylaert: Okay, perfect.
 
 Aline Muylaert: Good afternoon, everybody! I'm so happy to see many faces. I know that also, probably tomorrow is a bank holiday in the US, so really nice to see people here on a, let's say, special Monday. I'll go ahead and share my screen and share what we will be
 
 Aline Muylaert: Talking about, today, let me put this in,
 
 Aline Muylaert: slideshow. So yeah, today we'll be talking about solving problems with the public, something that is very close to our hearts at Go Vocal, as Aguira already introduced to you. I'm the co-founder of Go Vocal, and we now work for 10 years in digital democracy, digital community engagement.
 
 Aline Muylaert: Mostly with local governments, And we started in Belgium.
 
 Aline Muylaert: But we're now active all over the world, and also in the US. Now, a short introduction of our agenda for today. I will explain you a bit more about who we are at Govocal, how our platform works, some case studies, but then together with Karen, we will dive into how Hilorot is actually doing
 
 Aline Muylaert: this, solving problems with the public through technology and AI with the GoVocal platform, and then we're very much looking forward to your questions, so please drop them in the chat or the Q&A so that we can take them afterwards. We'll see how long this will take, probably 30 to 40 minutes, and then we'll go to the Q&A.
 
 Aline Muylaert: So let me start with introducing you Go Vocal. Some of you might already know us previously under our name Citizen Lab, but we rebranded 2 years ago to Go Vocal, and in the past 10 years, we have worked with more than 600 governments worldwide, and have engaged more than 2,000 or 2 million people, sorry. And you can see some logos here.
 
 Aline Muylaert: here on the slide. So, as I said, we started in Belgium, but we're active in many European countries.
 
 Aline Muylaert: working with quite some capital cities, such as Oslo, Copenhagen, Vienna, quite some London boroughs, but also now since 3-4 years? Quite active in the US,
 
 Aline Muylaert: with, like, some bigger cities, such as Kansas City, St. Louis.
 
 Aline Muylaert: Salt Lake City. I was still in New York City myself two weeks ago, so we have a big team there, so please reach out if you also want to learn a bit more about our work in the U.S, but we thought for today, it might be actually nice to inspire you with a more exotic case from Denmark, and inspire you on how we
 
 Aline Muylaert: do community engagement in Europe.
 
 Aline Muylaert: Now, before I give the floor to Karen, some slides to explain to you how GoVocal works, maybe also good to highlight that we've
 
 Aline Muylaert: been ranked this year the first platform by People Powered. Maybe some of you might know this organization and their ranking, but they kind of compare, globally digital participation tools, so we're very happy to be named a top tool in terms of functionalities.
 
 Aline Muylaert: And I think to really set the stage for today, and talking about this topic of solving problem with the public, one of the reasons why I, as a co-founder, started Go Vocal is because I really believe that community engagement can be more inclusive, continuous, and strategic. If we talk to local governments, they are often already doing community
 
 Aline Muylaert: the engagement, but technology can really help them to reach more people, do it more often, and on important topics, so really trying to solve
 
 Aline Muylaert: problems with the public, so that in the end, we build more trust in our governments, in our democracy. So that's really kind of the mission that we are striving for at Go Vocal, and we're so honored to be working with more than hundreds of governments worldwide. Also important to stress that we are a B Corp, so we really try to put this
 
 Aline Muylaert: Mission central to our, work.
 
 Aline Muylaert: Now, what do we see, like, next to this mission, what do we see as one of the main problems when looking at, participation? You can call it citizen participation, community engagement, community participation. We often see that governments are facing siloed participation. They have lots of fragmented tools.
 
 Aline Muylaert: inefficient processes across teams, across departments, and that often leads to reduced and transactional engagements. So actually not being able to solve problems with the public because we are not properly engaging them.
 
 Aline Muylaert: Now, that's something that at Govocal, we try to solve through a central management
 
 Aline Muylaert: platform, and over the few… over the past few years, we've really also evolved from a tool that is collecting input online
 
 Aline Muylaert: to trying to incorporate all these other channels, so paper forms, speech-to-text from meetings with residents, so really trying to be very agnostic to how a government is collecting input.
 
 Aline Muylaert: So that we can be as inclusive as possible, and eventually help drive repeated engagement. And we do, through that, we do that through our platform, which is a central hub for all participation projects. We'll see immediately a few of the projects that, Hilerot in Denmark is managing on their platform.
 
 Aline Muylaert: But, if you look at our platform, it really works in 3 ways. There's an engagement part.
 
 Aline Muylaert: Which has a lot of different tools, to manage your community.
 
 Aline Muylaert: And then we have a back office that is really strong, that also gave us this high score by People Powered, and that's where you can actually manage all that input, take decisions, and especially in the last step, the AI sense-making really comes in, because if you're gathering lots of input, how do you make sense out of it? How do you cluster it?
 
 Aline Muylaert: How do you, summarize it.
 
 Aline Muylaert: So that's a bit, in a nutshell, how our platform works. Now, if we look at the toolbox, we often structure this based on the IEP2 spectrum of participation, which probably many of you know, and the higher you go up on this ladder, the more influence you give to your residents, to your community, to actually have a say
 
 Aline Muylaert: Eventually, in the decisions being made. And we at Govocal try to have the tools at every level, we continuously keep developing these, these methods.
 
 Aline Muylaert: And I think today we'll be talking about a few of these also with CADIN. Surveys is still really important. I already talked about the paper forms, taking voices along, so voice-based participation. Then a lot of what we do is also prioritization.
 
 Aline Muylaert: ideation, and eventually, we also try to really empower people to make decisions on our platform through the liberative features and parts of their budgeting. So reach out afterwards if you want to have more of, more explanation on some of these tools.
 
 Aline Muylaert: Now, talking about inclusiveness, I think it's interesting to highlight a few things that we do. First of all, language accessibility is really important to us. I think, especially in the US, this is a really big topic. How can we make sure that people can,
 
 Aline Muylaert: Yeah, participate in their own language.
 
 Aline Muylaert: So that's something that we really try to work on a lot.
 
 Aline Muylaert: Representativeness as well. We don't necessarily try to strive for representativeness, but we want to show you how representative the input is. So also, later, we will look at an example of, Hillary, where we can see, like, okay, what is the age where people are participating in, and who might we be missing? And if you do, then, physical participation, offline events.
 
 Aline Muylaert: You might actually make sure that
 
 Aline Muylaert: in the end, you are reaching a quite representative input. And then, as I've already said, it's really important to blend with offline channels, so you can see here a screenshot of how we incorporate
 
 Aline Muylaert: paper into our platform so that we can scan forms through OCR technology and take that all along.
 
 Aline Muylaert: Last thing are our AI summaries. I know this is a case about AI, we will dive a bit into it, but there's, like, yeah, a few big parts to our AI.
 
 Aline Muylaert: Which is, on one hand, we help clients cluster a lot of inputs, so you can see that here we help them tag based on sentiment, based on tags, and so on. But then we also help them summarize all that input, and you can actually ask questions based on the input. So we're not…
 
 Aline Muylaert: Let's say, building our own models, but we're building a kind of layer on top of,
 
 Aline Muylaert: these generative AI models that can then actually allow you to interact with the input that you are getting, and that can be
 
 Aline Muylaert: Open ideas, there can be open answers to surveys, so that you eventually can save a lot of time on processing this.
 
 Aline Muylaert: Now, enough about the platform, maybe shortly, why do we feel like we are helping governments well? Because we are helping them to modernize participation. We really believe in this repeated engagement so that we can keep a constant community pulse.
 
 Aline Muylaert: I've already talked about our insights, and Katen will also talk about the need of working smarter across teams. I think
 
 Aline Muylaert: Community engagement can only be really powerful if, you really see this as kind of a…
 
 Aline Muylaert: Yeah, citywide initiative where many different, teams or governments and, departments are involved.
 
 Aline Muylaert: And then on the right-hand side, you can see a quote from Denise Srachi, the current mayor of the city of Lancaster in Pennsylvania, that said, like, okay, this platform really helped us to build trust.
 
 Aline Muylaert: By showing that we're listening, and showing what we are doing with their input, but also explaining what we couldn't do. So that's, I think, really important. It's not about just doing what people are saying, but it's about explaining why you, or how you take their feedback along.
 
 Aline Muylaert: Now, enough about the sales pitch, almost. I do want to leave you now with a few cases before we dive into the Hillerrod case, and I want to just show you the wide range of topics that we are working on at Govocal, so we do a lot of
 
 Aline Muylaert: strategy and budgeting, also planning and placemaking. I think most of the topics and projects that we
 
 Aline Muylaert: Support on our platform are actually linked to urban planning, mobility, so this is a really important category. Then also quite some climate, projects. Participatory budgeting is quite popular in,
 
 Aline Muylaert: in Europe, but also more and more in the US, let's say. And then, Copenhagen is a nice example of how bottom-up we can actually collect signatures to allow for proposals to be posted on the Council agenda.
 
 Aline Muylaert: Now, talking about participatory budgeting, I want to highlight one project in the US, which is the St. Louis case. Probably some of you have heard
 
 Aline Muylaert: when the Rams moved out of the city, they got a big settlement of $250 million, and the city council actually couldn't agree on how to spend it.
 
 Aline Muylaert: So they reached out to us, and they started a big participation process where people could, on one hand, first give in ideas, on how this budget should be spent.
 
 Aline Muylaert: Then all of these ideas were clustered into priorities.
 
 Aline Muylaert: And then these priorities were presented back to the community, and then they could vote on these priorities. And we actually helped them reach a decision on this. So the number one priority that came out of this was investing in water infrastructure. The city council was quite surprised
 
 Aline Muylaert: with that outcome, because they would… they were expecting, like, more other topics. But so that just shows that involving the public, crowdsourcing first very big, and then involving them in prioritizing can really help, unlock, let's say, the…
 
 Aline Muylaert: yeah, the resources that there are available in the community, and I think this is a really good example of how a platform or community engagement can actually really help solve problems with the public.
 
 Aline Muylaert: Now, this is really my last slide. I just want to leave you with, already kind of…
 
 Aline Muylaert: one principle that we believe is really key when we want to solve problems with the public, and Katen will also talk about, is what we call the culture of engagement.
 
 Aline Muylaert: Platforms are nice, tools are nice, technology is nice, but eventually it all really comes down to the people working with these technologies within the governments.
 
 Aline Muylaert: And we really see that a culture of engagement can make or break the success. And so if we break that down, we are looking at ambition from elected officials and management, a strong internal setup.
 
 Aline Muylaert: And processes, and of course, the right skills and resources.
 
 Aline Muylaert: And I'm happy that with this webinar, we can actually contribute to that last pillar. But without further ado, now the floor to, Karen for her to explain you a bit more about how Hilorot Komune is solving problems with
 
 Aline Muylaert: The public. Karen, the floor is yours.
 
 Karin Juhl: Thank you very much. Can you hear and see? I think it should be fine.
 
 Aline Muylaert: Yes.
 
 Karin Juhl: Well, yeah, my name is Karen Yule, and I've worked for the Hillel Municipality for nearly 30 years, and have been working with engagement of the community for all the time I've… I've been in the municipality.
 
 Karin Juhl: And in 2018, after the election there, we had a,
 
 Karin Juhl: a special group of politicians and citizens that sat together for 4 years and talked about how to improve the engagement of the community. And one of the things they decided after
 
 Karin Juhl: The first year was to, think about getting a digital platform, and so we got into, Go Vocal.
 
 Karin Juhl: So we have had it since, 2020.
 
 Karin Juhl: And so we have,
 
 Karin Juhl: some, to, to some extent, some, good, experience and, practice, about it. We have,
 
 Karin Juhl: We have, had…
 
 Karin Juhl: about 50 projects, that has actually come into something. We have also a lot of trials and things we thought, oh, we'll do this and that, and then it comes out to, no, it's not the best way.
 
 Karin Juhl: So that's why it says like this. We have, 4,510 users, that's, that's about 8% of, our, of everybody in the municipality, including children.
 
 Karin Juhl: So that's kind of nice. And, yeah, we have been since, yeah, 2019, we're the first year.
 
 Karin Juhl: So, we are… Working in an area where people are… Pretty high educated.
 
 Karin Juhl: And, the…
 
 Karin Juhl: They also have, they live in nice houses, many of them, and have nice incomes. So it's, it's, it's a place where
 
 Karin Juhl: people want to go and live. So it's very… it's expanding a lot, and we will come into some of the troubles there is with an expanding city, where the castle, you can see in the picture, is taking up one-fourth of the central town. It gives some troubles.
 
 Karin Juhl: Next.
 
 Karin Juhl: This is a… this shows the platform and what we have right now on it, and it's, it's solar power plants, and it's traffic.
 
 Karin Juhl: And it's the budget that we every year, do something to spread out and have
 
 Karin Juhl: To have income, to sayings from the communities about,
 
 Karin Juhl: All the economy in the budget every year.
 
 Karin Juhl: So that's what we do. Next.
 
 Karin Juhl: Yeah, one of the biggest things we have had, recently is this, is this…
 
 Karin Juhl: a project about, green mobility and less congestation, and that is a huge trouble in, in, in Hillel. Actually,
 
 Karin Juhl: It is so bad that people say it's more easy to get to come across Manhattan than it is to come through Hillel.
 
 Karin Juhl: And, and they, and they're actually right. And it will just, go worse. Because we have had a lot of, companies.
 
 Karin Juhl: that has come to the town. For the last 5 years. We've had 5,000 more cars, that has to come in in the morning and out in the afternoon, so people are sitting in these lines for a long time.
 
 Karin Juhl: And we're not so used to that in Denmark.
 
 Karin Juhl: But, with this big trouble, that is, influencing, you know, many citizens' daily life.
 
 Karin Juhl: we had a perfect scene for people to get engaged in this problem, what is to do? Because, of course, we can buy, we can build more roads. It's very expensive, but we can do it.
 
 Karin Juhl: But in the central part of town, there is no place for more roads. So, so what, we had,
 
 Karin Juhl: a wide range of, of, ways that we were in engaging with the community about it. We used all the tools that is in, in Go Vocal.
 
 Karin Juhl: And we, also, had, meetings, physical meetings with the citizens. And so, to, many of the politicians, big surprise, people actually,
 
 Karin Juhl: know, kind of what to do, and they were… there was a very clear answer.
 
 Karin Juhl: And that was that we have to bike more, and we have to go on the…
 
 Karin Juhl: We have to use the collective transport systems
 
 Karin Juhl: Yeah, so that is kind of… have been a game changer also, for the politicians.
 
 Karin Juhl: that now has to think about how do we actually do that? How do we talk with people and engage people in changing their habits? And I think GoVocal will be a big part of that, too.
 
 Karin Juhl: So it's not only that we can get answers from people, but we can maybe also use the platform to reach out to people and talk with them about how do we
 
 Karin Juhl: Actually, then, changed our habits to get more on the bike, and more, when it's the short, short, trips.
 
 Karin Juhl: Under 2 kilometers, for instance.
 
 Karin Juhl: And yeah, how to do that. So that was a big success, I think, and we are going to work with that, also the coming years.
 
 Aline Muylaert: Kat and I already skipped to the next one so that people can see how the platform looked like for this particular project, and maybe it's also good to hear, show a bit, like, how the AI analysis works
 
 Aline Muylaert: in the back that we have used for this, this project that we… I mean, that we collected lots of input on.
 
 Karin Juhl: Yeah. This is… when we use the AI, you can see we only used it for a project at the time. So when you see the numbers, it doesn't look so impressive, but because we had a lot of projects.
 
 Karin Juhl: we had actually, like, more than a thousand… yeah, we have 1,400 voices in, through all kinds of, engagement activities. But,
 
 Karin Juhl: what is fantastic about the AI sense-making is that we can ask open questions, so we don't have to kind of guess.
 
 Karin Juhl: what is this about for, the citizens? When we make a traditional, oh, what's it called again? Questionary?
 
 Karin Juhl: You know, we, we, we kind of easily get into the tradition about,
 
 Karin Juhl: thinking we know what this question is about, and then we ask from our logic all the questions. But here we, with the AI, sense-making, module, we could, ask more open questions, and people could make,
 
 Karin Juhl: Suggestions into the project.
 
 Aline Muylaert: And, with…
 
 Karin Juhl: with a lot of, lot of, lots of, lots of inputs. I mean, many, many pages. So if we had to,
 
 Karin Juhl: to work with this in a traditional way, it would have taken all too many resources. We were a…
 
 Karin Juhl: we are, not so many people that work with this, so, so it would have been taking too much… too many resources. So what we could do now is we could take all this, project by project, we could take all this data.
 
 Karin Juhl: And see, with the auto-tack, which you see out in the… in the left.
 
 Karin Juhl: Yeah, here in the left, you can auto-tag… auto-tag what is people actually talking about?
 
 Karin Juhl: And then you can ask for questions about these things. What are they talking about? And what is very important, now we have AI, we have had AI for a couple of years, but still, we have to check up that it's actually not,
 
 Karin Juhl: hallucinating anything or, getting things wrong. So, we have this fantastic thing where we can,
 
 Karin Juhl: When it's due the summary, we can, get into, the, data, the original data, and see, is it actually a, sensible, resume that it is making.
 
 Karin Juhl: So, it has been fantastic in this, we couldn't have done it without it.
 
 Karin Juhl: That's for sure.
 
 Aline Muylaert: Karen, you want me to move to the proposals, or back to that first table?
 
 Karin Juhl: I think you can move to the proposals.
 
 Karin Juhl: So, one of the things we have had for many years, also before we had, Go Vocal, is,
 
 Karin Juhl: citizen's proposal. And when now I say a citizen proposal, it's for everybody, it's not like you need to have some legal paper to make it. It's, it's okay. As long as you live in Hilor Kumoun, you can make it.
 
 Karin Juhl: So, you can make a proposal.
 
 Karin Juhl: And, if it gets more than 450 votes in, 6 months.
 
 Karin Juhl: It is, the… the deal that then the… the… the mayor and the…
 
 Karin Juhl: And the government, the local government, has to take, to take a serious debate on,
 
 Karin Juhl: On the case. It's not like we have to do what people say, as also a lean, planet, but we have to talk about it.
 
 Karin Juhl: So, and also, there is a lot of people that actually propose things where they never get so many, votes.
 
 Karin Juhl: But even if they only have one vote or two votes, I look them over, and I go to the…
 
 Karin Juhl: to the department that has the area of the question, or the proposal, and I ask them, is… are we doing anything in this area, or is it this topic? Do we have anything on that? So we can kind of be proactive about
 
 Karin Juhl: the suggestions that… that people come with, and I think, that, that is, that is something that makes the…
 
 Karin Juhl: The citizen feel that we take, things serious.
 
 Karin Juhl: Yeah.
 
 Karin Juhl: So, yeah.
 
 Karin Juhl: We also… yeah.
 
 Karin Juhl: We also have challenges in the municipality available, of course we have that.
 
 Karin Juhl: And, with, the platform Go Vocal, I cannot stress enough that it's actually a very easy platform to use. I mean, if I work with colleagues,
 
 Karin Juhl: Especially the younger colleagues.
 
 Karin Juhl: wow, are they just fast in grabbing? How do you put up projects? How do you work with it? It's a very logical and very easy system to work with, even with the many extra features that has
 
 Karin Juhl: come in the last years. I have just done it today, on a big, big project we have
 
 Karin Juhl: on the green three-part we have in Denmark, very little nature.
 
 Karin Juhl: Because we have so much farming land, so we have to do something about this, and that is a big national project, and it is really going to take a lot of community engagement to
 
 Karin Juhl: To make, voluntary, people voluntary, give up their farming land and turn it into nature.
 
 Karin Juhl: And that I've been sitting with today with a young guy, and boy, was he just fast in grabbing how to make
 
 Karin Juhl: this, pretty complicated project he has, so, that's nice. But…
 
 Karin Juhl: To get, to get the leaders and the colleagues to gain knowledge about the platform is, of course.
 
 Karin Juhl: difficult. I mean, it's like, you have… I have to put people into the platform when it's actual for them to use it. I mean, it's not something you,
 
 Karin Juhl: can just put people into, like, if you have to use it in 2 or 3 years, I'm just telling you about it, you have to do it right before they have to use it. So,
 
 Karin Juhl: We do that.
 
 Karin Juhl: It is… in Denmark, we have many rules about community engagement in the technical area, where on the other areas, it's more…
 
 Karin Juhl: It's more voluntary for the…
 
 Karin Juhl: for the municipality to actually engage people. So they had… they don't have the same traditions as they have in the technical area. So also in… in the municipality of Hillel, it's… it's many, it's many…
 
 Karin Juhl: Projects we have about how to, how to use the territory, and not so much about
 
 Karin Juhl: How to do with, children and youngsters, how to do in the social, areas, but it's coming slowly, and the more people get to know the platform, the more,
 
 Karin Juhl: The more they like it.
 
 Karin Juhl: Yeah. So, the challenge number 3 is to get the internal buy-in from all the stakeholders. It's like this, and I think that will be also, something you can recognize.
 
 Karin Juhl: The local, politicians, they are very eager to engage.
 
 Karin Juhl: the citizens and the community. They really want to know what would the citizens like, what would the community like.
 
 Karin Juhl: And, it's also my,
 
 Karin Juhl: impression that, people that is working, face-to-face with the citizens or working, with the projects are actually also
 
 Karin Juhl: pretty interested in engaging the community. Where we have the… where we have the challenge, or face the challenge, is in the management, layer.
 
 Karin Juhl: It can be,
 
 Karin Juhl: Yeah, it's challenging to be a manager in municipalities and in government, local governments. It's a very stressful job, and,
 
 Karin Juhl: To have this, a little bit dark horse that comes in with all the suggestions and the opinions from the citizens.
 
 Karin Juhl: That often make the politicians change a little bit their look at things. So it, of course, makes things better, but it also makes it more complicated. And it's not…
 
 Karin Juhl: Always that, that the management, think that's a good idea, to say it how it is.
 
 Karin Juhl: Yeah So, the next slide.
 
 Karin Juhl: Yeah. Some of the things I have done to, to engage the, the municipality is to,
 
 Karin Juhl: follow along in the development plans to identify possible projects. It is to look every time we… every year when we make the budget, the politicians, they…
 
 Karin Juhl: they, put in a… in a big book, what are we going to do the next year? And I usually look at that, and because people who don't know the platform, they… they're maybe not… they… maybe they can't see
 
 Karin Juhl: the potentials and possibilities for citizen engagement in their project, but it's easier to see when you know the platform and when you have worked with community engagement for many years. So often I can go to the
 
 Karin Juhl: to the people working with a special task where I can see that,
 
 Karin Juhl: citizen engagement or community engagement would be a good idea. And talk with them, and take a meeting with them, and say, we have actually a tool here, which would be good if you want to… to, kind of form your project also from what the citizens and the community think that they
 
 Karin Juhl: would like. Also, because it's actually… we have, in Hillel, but I think it is all over the world like this, big groups of people are actually very smart. It's also,
 
 Karin Juhl: It's actually also, you can see that in science, that you can take a very, harmonious,
 
 Karin Juhl: educated group, and put a… give them a task, and they come up with some solutions, yes, but if you give it to a very diverse group, they actually come up with the best solutions. So, so that's another argument for involving the citizens.
 
 Karin Juhl: As I said, number two is that I ask these leaders for provision… provisional facts for topics in the citizens' suggestions. I just told you about that before.
 
 Karin Juhl: And, a very good idea is, of course, to have project groups to, to also have inputs to how to design the community engagement, from different, points of views.
 
 Karin Juhl: it's actually the same story all over again. It's much better to… to have a group, to… to make…
 
 Karin Juhl: the community engagement, it makes it better, more strong. They have also more channels to actually get hold of people, because that's another
 
 Karin Juhl: challenge it is, people don't, wake up in the morning and think, oh, I have to go in to look at Go Vocal and see what's new. You have to find ways to, actually get them in there.
 
 Karin Juhl: And, SOBE can, of course, be a, be a solution. But,
 
 Karin Juhl: Yeah, it's… it's much better if, the people, you work with in the project group actually has, channels to, the…
 
 Karin Juhl: To the… to… to the citizens,
 
 Karin Juhl: in other ways. Maybe they have a lot of… a long email list, maybe they have some small rooms where they meet also digitally with the citizens or something, where they can actually
 
 Karin Juhl: Yeah, get them in on the platform.
 
 Karin Juhl: Yep.
 
 Aline Muylaert: Thank you so much, Karen, for sharing your light on how, Hiloroticomuna is engaging with, with the public. Now we're very happy to take on questions, and maybe looking at,
 
 Aline Muylaert: Perfect. That was, innovation.
 
 Agueda Quiroga (InnovateUS): I will turn off… first, I will turn off the…
 
 Agueda Quiroga (InnovateUS): The recording, give me a moment.
